name: Jamu

lead: Jamu is a traditional Indonesian herbal medicine made from roots, bark, flowers, seeds, leaves and fruits such as turmeric, ginger, temulawak and tamarind. Javanese tradition links jamu and the lulur body treatment to the beauty routines of royal court women, and jamu drinks are widely taken as everyday wellness and skin-and-body tonics.

In appearance terms, people use it as a drink or body preparation to support skin, freshness and general well-being. Published research has mostly examined individual ingredients such as turmeric species and the chemistry of jamu plants; there are few clinical trials of jamu as a beauty practice.

paras: Jamu is commonly drunk as a freshly prepared herbal drink, sold by street vendors known as mbok jamu or jamu gendong, or taken as factory-made sachets, capsules and liquids. Turmeric-and-tamarind drinks (kunyit asam) are among the best-known types. A separate tradition uses lulur, a traditional body treatment, alongside jamu. Practitioners describe formulas tailored to age and need and used regularly rather than as a one-off.

Indonesian regulator BPOM prohibits pharmaceutical drugs in jamu, yet it has seized products found to contain drugs such as sildenafil, tadalafil, NSAIDs or corticosteroids. The US FDA and other regulators have likewise reported hidden drugs in some imported products. Toxicology reviews also discuss contaminants such as aflatoxins and plant constituents of concern, and quality varies in mass-produced products.

angle.text: Practitioners use jamu drinks, and the related lulur body treatment, as a long-running beauty and wellness tradition aimed at skin and overall freshness. The look-related benefits are those claimed in tradition; research has focused on ingredients such as turmeric.

lead: Jamu is a traditional Indonesian medicine system, mostly herbal, made from roots, bark, flowers, seeds, leaves and fruits, with some preparations also using honey, royal jelly, milk or eggs [1]. It is most closely associated with Java, where women sellers known as mbok jamu traditionally carry bottled drinks through neighbourhoods [1]. Factory-made versions now come as sachets, tablets, capsules and liquids [1].

Jamu matters to appearance because it has long been tied to beauty and body care. Javanese tradition credits jamu and the lulur body treatment for the beauty of women of the royal courts, and jamu products have been linked to the cosmetics business [1]. People today take jamu drinks such as turmeric-and-tamarind blends as everyday tonics for skin and a healthy look, and herbal ingredients such as turmeric species are discussed in reviews for skin-related traditional uses [2].

Research on jamu consists mainly of ingredient-level pharmacology, chemistry and safety reviews rather than trials of jamu as a beauty practice [2][3][4]. UNESCO inscribed Jamu wellness culture on its Intangible Cultural Heritage list in December 2023 [1].
infobox: Fresh drinks, sachets, capsules, tablets, liquids

paras: Jamu is described as a holistic tradition that aims to keep the body in balance, drawing on a hot-and-cold framework found across Malay and Javanese health beliefs [5]. Preparations may be a single plant or a mixture, and are traditionally ground with a mortar and pestle and boiled or steeped [1]. Common ingredients include rhizomes such as ginger, turmeric, temulawak and galangal, leaves such as brotowali and secang, fruits such as tamarind and key lime, and spices such as cinnamon and fennel [1].
Indonesian government categories separate traditional jamu from standardised herbal medicines and from fitofarmaka, or clinically tested phytopharmaceuticals [6].

Wikipedia notes that jamu may date to the Mataram kingdom about 1,300 years ago, with a mortar and pestle from the Liyangan site (about the 8th to 10th centuries) suggesting an established practice [1]. A Mataram medicine book from around 1700 is said to list about 3,000 recipes, and the 1814 Serat Centhini describes some concoctions [1]. European physicians recorded jamu from the 17th century, and a 1911 household handbook by Kloppenburg-Versteegh was widely used in the Dutch East Indies [1].

Jamu was formally recognised by Indonesian physicians in the 1940s, a Jamu Committee was formed in 1944, and in 2019 it was recognised as national intangible cultural heritage before the December 2023 UNESCO listing [1]. A 1999 editorial described jamu as an Indonesian herbal tradition with a long past and an uncertain future [7].

sections.h: Use for beauty and body care
paras: Javanese tradition credits jamu and lulur, a traditional body lotion, with the beauty of royal court women [1]. Today jamu brands are tied to cosmetics, and some products are marketed for sexual wellness [1]. Reviews of Javanese turmeric (temulawak), a core jamu ingredient, list skin eruptions among its traditional uses [2].

A 2021 toxicology review discussed hazards from adulteration with active pharmaceutical ingredients and from genotoxic and carcinogenic constituents in some jamu [3]. Indonesia's regulator BPOM bans drug ingredients in jamu, yet it regularly seizes products found to contain sildenafil, tadalafil, NSAIDs or corticosteroids [1]. The US FDA issued a 2022 notice about hidden drugs in a product called Tawon Liar, and Singapore and Saudi Arabia reported hidden drugs in another called Montalin [1]. A study of commercial jamu and makjun from Malaysia and Indonesia examined natural aflatoxin occurrence in such products [8].

No studies found on jamu as a beauty or appearance practice. Related research includes a review of the pharmacology of Javanese turmeric, an ingredient in jamu [2], a review of chemical constituents and bioactivities of jamu plants [4], and a 2024 randomised open-label trial of a poly-herbal galactagogue from Indonesia, which concerned breastfeeding rather than looks [9].
